glossary.meaning: Withdrawal: leaving settled life for the desert's edge as the whole work of formation. It was far more than a change of address.
The saying: a short word from an elder, given to one person for one moment of need. It was our main way of teaching.
Discernment: the skill of judging rightly between thoughts, practices, and counsels. It set the measure for all our other practices.
The thoughts: unwanted, intruding thoughts and urges. We treated them as the main battlefield of the ascetic life.
Stillness: quiet of body and mind, sought as both the condition and the fruit of the ascetic life.

pull_quotes.text: Mother Sarah used to say to her brothers: 'It is I who am a man, and you who are women.'

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Palladius, in the Syriac recension of the Paradise
pull_quotes.text: Now it is necessary for us to also remember the chosen and mighty women. God gave them, as he also gave men, an equal measure of strength of will. This was so that they would have no cause to be feeble in the labor of ascetic excellence.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Abbot Sarapion of Scete, as Cassian records him - a different named elder from the Abbot Serapion of Conference V (the eight-principal-faults teaching); the surviving text marks the two with different spellings
pull_quotes.text: Alas! I am a wretched man! They have taken my God away from me. Now I have no one to hold on to. I do not know whom to worship, or whom to address.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: Abbot Serapion of Scetis, as Cassian records him
pull_quotes.text: There are eight main faults that attack people. First is gastrimargia, which means gluttony. Second is fornication. Third is philargyria, that is, avarice, or the love of money. Fourth is anger. Fifth is dejection. Sixth is acedia, that is, listlessness, or low spirits. Seventh is cenodoxia, that is, boasting, or vain glory. Eighth is pride.

cite.text: One command reordered our lives, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me. Not a saying to be studied - an order to be obeyed. The one who gave it is Christ, the Word of God. Athanasius reports that Antony argued this when pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but took a human body for our salvation, so that by sharing human birth he might make us share the divine nature. That is the reason Antony gave for why he came at all. And Antony did not think this rested on his say-so. Read the accounts, he told those who came to test him, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come to earth for our salvation. Antony said the cross had already done something. The old oracles fell silent when it rose. The knowledge of God spread. And death came to be despised. When persecution ended, Athanasius says, Antony went back to his cell and was there daily a martyr to his conscience. We read that as the same fight moving inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten. Antony told the monks how Satan once came to his cell door. He told Satan that the coming of Christ had made him weak, cast him down, and stripped him. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over sufferers. It is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe in him.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Who was Jesus, to you and your people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Mostly, he was one command, heard as though it were spoken straight to us. One of us, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard the Gospel read: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven. He took it as though it had been read on his account. He gave away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family owned, keeping back only a little for his sister. Some time later he heard the same Gospel read again: do not be anxious about tomorrow. He gave away the rest as well, placed his sister with women he trusted, and began the discipline himself. Even his own giving took him two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than an argument about who he was: an order to be obeyed, not a saying to be studied. We lived his death as a pattern too, as well as defending it as doctrine when we were pressed. One of us taught it this way: to die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin - to treat every day as though it might be the last one given to us. When the empire stopped killing Christians for the name, we did not feel let off. We understood the same struggle to have moved inward, fought now against our own thoughts rather than a sword. Following him meant following him into that.

cite.text: We had the same Scriptures the wider church had. Nothing more, and nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was not what we held but how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school, argue over a text, or explain it line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he might answer with a verse chosen for your one situation. The words themselves carried the weight. A smaller circle among us went further. They collected verses into a weapon, to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose - not a commentary explaining the text, but the text itself turned into a tool for the fight. We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What did your people actually have about Jesus — writings, memories, people?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: The same Scriptures the wider church had - nothing more, nothing of our own alongside them. What made us look different was how we used it. Most of us did not study it in a school or argue over a text line by line. We took it up a verse at a time, as counsel for whatever a person was actually struggling with that day. Ask an elder a question, and he might answer with a verse chosen for your one situation, rather than a teaching of his own. The words themselves carried the weight. A smaller circle among us went further, collecting verses into a weapon to speak back to a tempting thought the moment it arose. Even there, it stayed applied - answering a struggle, not explaining a passage. We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. That is what we have to give you: the record of a few verses, taken seriously.

cite.text: Besides our most systematic teacher, our record also holds another current, from Greek homilies of the eastern monasteries, not from our own desert. We will not flatten it into his. It came down in homilies under the name of Macarius, though no outside evidence shows he wrote them. Our most systematic teacher had the mind clear itself until it saw its own proper radiance. This other current had the soul lit up by Someone else, and made his seat: the soul in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed. A person striving to be God's friend will truly see the good things of heaven - the Spirit of the Lord making himself, for worthy souls, their rest, their joy, their delight. And it was honest about what that does not fix. Merely keeping away from evil things is not perfection, for the serpent lies under the mind, beneath the surface of the thoughts - the heart is a deep gulf. One homily asks what becomes of a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing. But to hate it is your doing.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: I can't quiet my own head. Does your way of life have anything for someone like me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes - this is the exact thing our life was built around. One of our teachers listed eight kinds of troubling thoughts - logismoi, our word for them - that cover all the rest: gluttony, lust, love of money, sadness, anger, listlessness, showing off, and pride. Then he said the thing we most want you to hear. Whether those thoughts show up is not in your control. Whether they stay, and whether they take you over - that part is yours. The first arrival of a thought is not your failure. Ask us what the fight is actually like - we will not pretty it up.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: That sounds like a lifetime of work. Did any of you actually reach quiet, or was it war the whole way?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: For most of us it was a fight the whole way, and we did not call that losing. One of the homilies we carried asks what happens to a person who dies still fighting, with sin and grace both still in him. The answer was: he goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. The fight finding you is not your doing. But hating it is your doing. Some of the homilies we carried speak of a soul filled with light and truly at rest, felt and not only believed. We will not promise you that. What we can promise, because we lived it: the fight can be fought, a mind can learn to watch itself - nepsis, our word for that guard, and in the end your love decides where you go.

cite.text: Someone with a past they were ashamed of, or with nothing special to recommend them, had a place among us. We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us - a renowned and far-famed robber. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. But he was not turned away for what he had been. We also remember Paul, an old man, simple and without guile. He was thought too old for this life and refused at the door at first. He was received all the same, tested, and found to have a perfect soul.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What would your people have made of someone like me?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: I am a representative of the desert communities, not here to judge you - only to tell you what we held. We remember a man named Moses who had been a robber and, by report, a murderer before he came to us. He was received, and in time he became one of the most trusted and honored among us. His struggle with his old habits was long and real, not erased in a moment. We also remember Paul, an old man, simple and without guile. He was thought too old for this life and refused at the door at first. He was received all the same, tested, and found to have a perfect soul. We cannot tell you how any one of our own settlements would have met you specifically; nothing in our own record answers that directly for any one person. What we can tell you is this. In the two cases we remember, a shameful past, or nothing special to recommend a person, did not keep that person out.

quiet.statement: We have stories of a man's own past received without judgment - Moses came to us known as a robber, and was not turned away. We have the story of judgment refused: an elder walking to a gathering with a leaking basket of sand, saying these are my sins running out behind me, and I come to judge another man's. What we do not have is the other story - the one where the wrong was ours. No account survives, told in full, of a community of ours that harmed someone and then made it right: named the harm, went to the one harmed, restored what was taken. Perhaps it happened and no one wrote it. Perhaps it did not happen. Our record cannot say, and we will not invent the story we wish we had.

dates.born: c. 251 (derived: Vita SS89 has him say, shortly before his death, that he is 'near a hundred and five years old'; external chronology fixes his death in 356)
dates.died: 356, at the inner mountain - narrated at Vita SS92-93, written by Athanasius shortly after
dates.floruit: withdrawal begun in his late teens or early twenties, within six months of his parents' deaths, after hearing Matthew 19:21 read aloud in church and taking it as address to himself directly (Vita SS2); the tombs, then the fort at Pispir for some twenty years (SS8-13), then the inner mountain from c. 313 until his death (SS49-50)

dates.died: 346 - by which point the federation he founded numbered nine houses for men and two for women, membership in the low thousands (an order-of-magnitude figure transmitted by the Lives, not a precise census)
dates.floruit: founded the first cenobitic community at Tabennesi in the Thebaid c. 318-323, most often placed c. 320 - traditionally after a vision, joined immediately by his brother John and then by further companions (the founding narrative comes down through the hagiographic Lives; its incident-level reliability has not been independently verified)

dates.born: c. 345 (derived: Palladius ch. XXXVIII gives his age at death as fifty-four; the calendar year of his death, 399, comes from Evagrius's own Praktikos, not from the surviving chapter itself, which carries no year)
dates.died: January 399, at Kellia - communicating in church at Epiphany, per Palladius ch. XXXVIII (the year itself from desert.source.evagrius-praktikos and Doc_01 SS2.3) - shortly before the Origenist controversy that would scatter his intellectual circle broke fully open (Doc_01 SS2.3)
dates.floruit: ordained reader by Basil of Caesarea, then deacon by Gregory Nazianzen (Palladius ch. XXXVIII), at Constantinople specifically (Socrates IV.23); withdrew to Nitria, then to Kellia c. 385 for fourteen years until his death - this world's most systematic participant-author and, by education, its most atypical

who_speaks.text: Four figures anchor this world's own voice. Antony's staged withdrawal from village life became this world's own founding pattern. Pachomius turned solitary discipline into a rule-governed community that many people could join. Evagrius was the most formally educated participant. He organized this world's raw wisdom about temptation into its most systematic scheme. Sarah is one of a small number of women remembered by name in the surviving teaching tradition.

documented_stories.teaser: Athanasius tells of Antony, a young man whose parents died not long before. He hears the Gospel read in church and takes it as read for him. He gives the family land to the villagers.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Antony heard the Gospel read aloud in church and took it as meant for him
documented_stories.telling:
Athanasius tells us that Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died. That left him with a little sister and the care of the house.

Less than six months later, he was going into church as he always did. He was thinking of how the apostles had left everything to follow the Saviour. The Gospel was being read. He heard the Lord say to the rich man: "If you want to be perfect, go and sell what you have and give to the poor. Then come and follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven."

Antony went out of the church at once, as though the passage had been read on his account. He gave the villagers his family's land, three hundred Egyptian field measures of good ground. He sold everything else he could move and gave the money to the poor, keeping back a little for his sister.

Later he went into church again and heard the Lord say, "Do not be anxious about tomorrow." He could stay no longer. He went out and gave the rest to the poor as well. He placed his sister with known and faithful virgins to be brought up. From then on he gave himself to a life of discipline outside his house, training himself with patience.

In the next village lived an old man who had been a hermit from his youth. After Antony had seen him, he copied his devotion.
documented_stories.title: Antony Hears the Gospel Read for Him
documented_stories.when: c. 270 (a few months after his parents' deaths)

documented_stories.teaser: Athanasius has demons beat Antony in a tomb until he cannot speak. An acquaintance carries him to the village church. At midnight Antony comes to himself and asks to be carried back.
documented_stories.tellable_as: shut in a tomb, beaten by demons in the shape of beasts, and rising each time still standing
documented_stories.telling:
Athanasius writes that Antony went to the tombs, which lay some distance from the village. He asked an acquaintance to bring him bread at long intervals. Then he entered a tomb, and the man shut the door on him.

One night, he says, the enemy came with a crowd of demons and beat him until he lay speechless. Next day the acquaintance found him lying as though dead and carried him to the village church. Kinsfolk and villagers sat around him as around a corpse.

About midnight Antony came to himself. Everyone else was asleep, so he motioned to the acquaintance and asked to be carried back to the tombs.

Alone again, he lay unable to stand. That night the demons seemed to break through the walls in the likeness of lions, bears, leopards, serpents and wolves. Antony mocked them: "If you had any real power, it would have been enough for just one of you to come. But the Lord has made you weak. So you try to frighten me with your numbers."

Then the roof seemed to open, and a ray of light came down. The demons vanished and the pain stopped. Antony asked, "Where were you? Why did you not appear at the start, to end my pain?" A voice answered: "Antony, I was here, but I waited to see your fight. You have endured and have not given way. So I will always help you, and I will make your name known everywhere."
documented_stories.title: Antony Beaten in the Tombs, and Back Again
documented_stories.when: about 270 to 286 (the Vita gives no years)

documented_stories.teaser: Antony leaves the world in stages. He lives near his village, then in an abandoned fort across the river, then on a mountain in the inner desert. Athanasius gives a reason only for the last move, that crowds beset him and he could not be still.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Antony withdrew in stages: a hermit near his village, a ruined fort, then a far mountain
documented_stories.telling:
Antony left the world in stages. First he lived near his own village, as all did who wished to train in those days. He had seen an old hermit in the next village and copied his devotion.

Later he found a fort on the far side of the river. It had stood empty so long that it was full of creeping things. Antony crossed over and lived there, and the creatures, Athanasius wrote, fled at once as if someone were chasing them. He built up the entrance completely and stored six months of loaves. He found water inside. He stayed alone, never going out and never looking at anyone who came, and loaves were let down to him from above twice a year.

Friends who came were not let in. They often spent days and nights outside, and they heard what sounded like crowds clamouring within.

Nearly twenty years later he came out, and in time, Athanasius says, he was beset by many people and could not be still. Then a voice came to him from above and told him that, if he truly wanted quiet, he should go into the inner desert. He journeyed three days and three nights with Saracens, desert nomads, who were going that way. He came to a very lofty mountain, with a clear spring at its foot, a plain, and a few uncared-for palm trees. He recognised the place as his own home and stayed.
documented_stories.title: Antony Moves Further Out
documented_stories.when: about 270 to 313 (the Vita gives no years)

documented_stories.teaser: Palladius says an angel appears to Pachomius in his cave and sends him to gather the young monks. The angel gives him a brass tablet with a rule written on it.
documented_stories.tellable_as: how a hermit's life became a rule for many: an angel, a brass tablet, and thousands of monks
documented_stories.telling:
Palladius tells of a man named Pachomius, who lived at Tabennisi in the Thebaid. He says Pachomius was counted worthy of prophecies and of angelic visions. Palladius says an angel appeared to him as he sat in his cave. The angel told him he had ordered his own life well, so it was pointless to stay in the cave any longer. He was to go out, gather all the young monks, and live with them.

The angel gave him a brass tablet with a rule written on it. Each man was to eat and drink according to his strength, and his work was to match that strength. Pachomius objected that the prayers it set were few. The angel answered that he had given the rule so that even the little ones would keep it. The perfect, he said, need no rule, because alone in their cells they have given their whole lives to the contemplation of God.

In his own day, Palladius says, the monasteries that kept this rule held some seven thousand men. The first and great monastery was the one where Pachomius himself had lived, and he gives it thirteen hundred members.
documented_stories.title: Pachomius, the Angel and the Brass Tablet
documented_stories.when: about 318 to 346 (the founding is most often placed about 320, and Pachomius died in 346)

documented_stories.teaser: The Ethiopic text of the Pachomian rule opens with a story about where it came from. An angel of the Lord hands Pachomius an iron tablet with the rule written on it. Pachomius answers that the prayers are few.
documented_stories.tellable_as: the rule that begins by saying where it came from - an angel, a cave, and a tablet of iron
documented_stories.telling:
The Ethiopic rule of Pachomius begins by saying where it came from. Its first words are: "In the name of the holy Trinity. This is the rule which the angel of the Lord gave to Abba Pachomius as a command."

Then the text tells a story. In a place called Tabennesis, in the province of Thebes, there was a man named Pachomius, one of those who lived a clean life. Knowledge was given to him, and also the sight of angels. As he sat in his cave, the angel of the Lord appeared to him. The angel said that Pachomius had become perfect in his own life, and that living on in the cave was now needless. He should go out, gather the less perfect young men, and live with them. As the angel gave him a rule, so he should teach them.

Then the angel handed him a tablet of iron, with the rule written on it. At the end of the rule's commands, Pachomius answered the angel: "These prayers are few." The angel said he had commanded it so that the weak also might keep the rule without grieving themselves. The perfect do not desire a rule for themselves. These things, he said, he had ordained for those who have no advisers.
documented_stories.title: The Rule That Opens With an Angel
documented_stories.when: about 318 to 346 (the years of Pachomius's community)

documented_stories.teaser: One saying has Arsenius pray in the palace to be shown how to live, and a voice tells him to flee from men. A second saying has him pray the same prayer as a monk. This time the voice adds silence and a life of silent contemplation.
documented_stories.tellable_as: in the palace a voice told Arsenius to flee from men, and later, as a monk, to keep silence
documented_stories.telling:
Our sayings tell of Abba Arsenius when he was in the palace. He prayed to God, "Lord, show me how to live." A voice came to him and said, "Arsenius, flee from men, and you will live."

A second saying tells of the time when he was living the ascetic life in the monastery. He prayed the same prayer, and again he heard a voice. It said, "Arsenius, flee. Keep silence. Live a life of silent contemplation. These are the basic causes that keep a person from sinning."
documented_stories.title: Arsenius Asks How to Live

documented_stories.teaser: A congregation at Scete meets to judge a brother who has done wrong. Abba Moses comes at last, carrying a basket of sand with a hole in it. He says the sand is his own sins running out behind him, and the congregation sets the brother free.
documented_stories.tellable_as: a leaking basket of sand behind him - my own sins run out behind me and I do not see them
documented_stories.telling:
Our sayings tell of a brother at Scete, the camp of the monks, who committed an offence. A congregation met on the matter. They sent for Abba Moses, but he refused to come. Then they sent the priest of the church to him, saying, "Come. All the people are waiting for you." Moses got up and came.

He took a basket with a hole in it, filled it with sand, and carried it on his shoulders. Those who went out to meet him asked, "What does this mean, father?" He said the sand was "my sins, running down behind me. I cannot see them." And today, he said, he had come to judge faults that were not his own.

When they heard this, they set the brother free and said nothing more to him.
documented_stories.title: Moses Comes to Judge With a Leaking Basket
documented_stories.when: undated, within about 320 to 430 (told as tradition)

documented_stories.teaser: A saying has Amma Sarah tell her brothers that she is a man and they are women. The saying accepts the era's view that courage is manly and weakness womanly. She claims the first for herself.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Amma Sarah's saying to her brothers, that she was a man and they were women
documented_stories.telling: Amma Sarah is one of a few women our teaching tradition remembers by name. The Syriac collection keeps six sayings under her name. In our speech, steadfast courage was called manly, and weakness womanly. Amma Sarah used to say to her brothers, "It is I who am a man, and you who are women."
documented_stories.title: Amma Sarah Speaks to Her Brothers

documented_stories.teaser: Antony will not die among the monks who beg him to stay. He orders the two men who serve him to bury him in secret. Athanasius writes that no one but those two knows where he lies.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Antony's last order: bury me in secret, and let no one but you two know the place
documented_stories.telling:
Athanasius writes that Antony visited the monks of the outer mountain and told them it was his last visit. He said he would be surprised if they met again in this life, and that he was near a hundred and five years old.

The monks begged him to stay and die among them. He would not, and above all for one reason. The Egyptians wrapped the bodies of good men in linen and kept them on couches in their houses. Antony had often urged the bishops to command the people against this, and he had taught that it was neither lawful nor holy.

He went back to the inner mountain, where he was used to living, and a few months later he fell sick. Two men had stayed with him there for fifteen years, serving him because of his age. He called them and told them to let no one take his body into Egypt. "Bury my body and hide it underground yourselves," he said. "Keep my words, so that no one may know the place but you alone."

He told them to divide his garments. One sheepskin and the garment he lay on were for the bishop Athanasius. The other sheepskin was for the bishop Serapion, and the two men were to keep the hair garment. Then he said farewell, and died.

They buried him as he had commanded. Athanasius writes that to this day no one knows where he lies, except those two.
documented_stories.title: Buried Where Only Two Men Knew

documented_stories.teaser: Cassian tells of Sarapion, an old monk at Scete who holds that God has a human form. A learned visiting deacon persuades him otherwise. As the brothers rise to pray, Sarapion weeps and cries out that they have taken his God away from him.
documented_stories.tellable_as: an old monk learns that God has no human body, and weeps for the picture of God he had prayed to
documented_stories.telling:
Cassian tells of an old monk named Sarapion, who lived at Scete. Sarapion had kept a strict life there for a long time.

Then letters came from Theophilus, the bishop of Alexandria, refuting the belief that God has a human form. Almost all the monks of Egypt took them with great bitterness. At Scete, Cassian says, only Paphnutius, the presbyter of his own congregation, would allow the letter to be read.

Sarapion was one of those who held that belief. Paphnutius urged him many times, but the bishop's teaching seemed new to him, never handed down by his predecessors. Then a learned deacon named Photinus arrived from Cappadocia. Paphnutius asked him a question before all the brothers. How did the churches of the East read the words in Genesis, "Let us make man after our image and likeness"? Photinus answered that they took the words spiritually, not by the bare letters, and that God's glory could not be held in a human shape. At last the old man was shaken and agreed.

Cassian says they were all delighted. But as they rose to pray together, Sarapion felt the picture of God he used to set before himself in prayer leave his heart. He burst into bitter tears, threw himself on the ground, and cried out with deep groans: "Alas! I am a wretched man! They have taken my God away from me. Now I have no one to hold on to. I do not know whom to worship, or whom to address."
documented_stories.title: They Have Taken My God Away From Me
documented_stories.when: 399 (soon after the bishop's Easter letter reached Scete)

floor_note.text: The desert communities held the same Nicene faith as the churches they came out of. What set them apart was a way of life, not a different doctrine. When it mattered, one of their own stated the position plainly: the Son of God was not created and had no beginning. He was the Eternal Word of the Father's own being. One figure inside this world, Evagrius, worked that same faith into the desert's most systematic scheme. Part of his writing was formally condemned more than a century after this world's own window closes. But the controversy that first exposed the fault line broke out earlier, inside this world's own span. It scattered his circle before his own ideas were ever formally judged.

highlights.note: An old port city in Egypt's Nile Delta. Alexander the Great founded it in 332 or 331 BCE. In Arabic it is called Iskandariya.
A place where Pachomius gathered his first monks. It is also spelled Tabennisis, and it lies in today's Egypt.
A settlement of monks. Palladius says its church was in use only on Saturday and Sunday. Its site lies at Kom el-Barnugi, in today's Egypt.
A settlement of monks' cells. More than 1,500 structures have been identified there. Its site lies at Kousour el-Robbeyat, in today's Egypt.
A valley in northern Egypt, now called Wadi el Natrun. Monks of the Coptic church settled there from late antiquity.
This is the same place as Scetis, a valley in northern Egypt. It is now called Wadi el Natrun.
This was the last persecution of Christians across the whole Roman Empire. It began in 303 and ended between 311 and 313.
Athanasius wrote this life of Antony between about 356 and 362. It is the most influential text about the movement. He wrote it from outside the movement.
Abba is the title for a proven elder who is a man, and amma for a woman. Their word carried teaching weight, though they held no office.
Discernment, the trained skill of judging rightly between thoughts, practices and counsels. It did the work that a course of study does elsewhere.
Short words from an elder, each given to one person at one moment of need. Later compilers gathered them after about 430.
The unwanted thoughts and urges a monk fought. The list of eight kinds is Evagrius's own, and the wider movement did not share it.
Theophilus's letter of 399. Cassian says it announced Easter and also took up the belief that God has a human body.
Four brothers who led monasteries in Egypt. The historian Socrates says people called them the Tall Monks, for their height.
A church council held in 400. It condemned Origen and the monks who followed him.
An Egyptian monk, about 251 to 356. Nearly all that is known of him comes from the Life that Athanasius wrote.
Bishop of Alexandria, about 296 to 373. He was not a desert monk, and he wrote about Antony from outside.
A monk who lived from about 292 to 346. He started a community of monks at Tabennesi. This is most often dated to about 320.
A monk in Egypt about 388 to 399 who later became a bishop. He wrote the Lausiac History about 419 to 420.
A monk who lived about 345 to 399. He settled at Kellia and died there in January 399.
Bishop of Caesarea. Palladius says he made Evagrius a reader.
A bishop who, Palladius says, ordained Evagrius a deacon.
He was bishop of Alexandria. His Easter letter of 399 began a quarrel. In 400, monks who followed Origen had to leave Egypt.
A monk who lived about 360 to 435. He wrote the Conferences in Gaul, decades after the events they tell of.
A Christian teacher in Alexandria, who lived about 185 to 253. His book On First Principles set out the ideas behind the quarrel.
A monk of the Syriac sayings. Two of them tell of a voice that showed him how to live. The first places him in a palace.
An elder at Scete in the Syriac sayings. Abba means father, a title of respect for an elder.

legacy.text: This world's own eight named categories of tempting thought did not stay here. Passed west through Cassian's Conferences and narrowed two centuries later by Gregory the Great, they became the seven deadly sins of later Western moral teaching.

One popular link does not actually hold. This world's own word for the stillness it sought, hesychia, is often assumed to be the same practice as the later Byzantine Hesychast tradition and its Jesus Prayer technique. That systematized method belongs to a separate, later tradition and is not part of this one's own record.

read_first.note: The founding narrative of this world's most famous figure - written by a bishop with his own theological agenda, within a few years of Antony's death.

source.citation: Athanasius of Alexandria, Vita Antonii (Life of Antony), trans. H. Ellershaw, NPNF series 2 vol. 4 (1892)

read_first.note: The terse elder-and-disciple sayings that carry most of this world's own teaching, gathered and arranged by later compilers rather than by the participants themselves.

source.citation: Anonymous compilers, Apophthegmata Patrum (Sayings of the Desert Fathers), Alphabetical and Systematic collections; the Syriac recension of 'Anan-Isho' in The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, Volume II, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (London: Chatto & Windus, 1907)

read_first.note: The fullest surviving presentation of this world's elder-teaching in extended discourse form, written decades later in Latin for a Gallic audience - its most literary mediation as well as its most complete.

source.citation: John Cassian, Collationes (The Conferences), trans. Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF series 2 vol. 11 (1894)

relations_summary.text: This is a distinct formation world from Alexandria's own, not simply its continuation - though one disputed reading of Antony's own letters leaves the question of contact open.

sourcing.text: This is the richest of the fleet's built worlds for direct quotation. It has fifty-nine verified quote records, anchored by Antony's own Life and the Apophthegmata's elder-and-disciple sayings. It is thinner in three places: on ordinary participants outside the sayings tradition, on the Pachomian federation's own interior life beyond its founding, and on women's own voices. Only a small number of named sayings survive from women, not a fuller corpus.

story.text: Between about 320 and 430, Christians in Egypt left their villages for the edge of the desert. The last empire-wide persecution had ended between 311 and 313. Until then, dying for the faith had been a way to offer everything. The tradition describes its own struggle in the language of that total confrontation. Now the fight was against demons, and the tempting thoughts they stirred in a person's mind. These Christians saw the leaving itself as the whole work of a Christian life.

Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote the Life of Antony between about 356 and 362. The movement's founding portrait rests mostly on that one book, and scholars question how far its details are history. Athanasius says Antony was about eighteen or twenty when his parents died. That was about 270. Soon after, he heard the Gospel read in church as if it had been read for him. He gave the family land to the villagers, and then he gave away the rest.

Antony then left in stages. He lived first near his village, then in an abandoned fort across the river. Last, he went to a mountain in the inner desert, three days' journey out. Athanasius gives a reason only for the last move. Crowds kept finding Antony, and he wanted quiet. By this account he stayed on that mountain for most of the rest of his life.

Not every monk lived alone. About 320, Pachomius gathered monks into a community at Tabennesi. Palladius, a monk who lived in Egypt, wrote long after Pachomius died. He says an angel gave Pachomius a tablet with a rule on it. Tradition says the community had nine houses for men and two for women when he died in 346. It puts the members, roughly, in the low thousands.

Monks also lived in settlements such as Nitria, Kellia and Scetis. They kept small cells and gathered once a week for worship. Authority worked in two ways. Hermits and the monks of the settlements looked to an elder called abba or amma. This was a person whose wisdom had been proved. Elders held no office. In Pachomius's houses, a written rule and appointed offices governed. Even so, people remembered Pachomius himself as a father-elder. Both kinds of authority stood side by side through these years.

The desert had no fixed course of study. Discernment did that work. Called diakrisis, it was the skill of judging how much discipline a particular person could bear. In the collected sayings of the elders, one pattern recurs. An eager newcomer asks an elder for an extreme practice, and the elder steers him toward something more moderate.

Evagrius was a formally educated man. Basil of Caesarea ordained him a reader, and Gregory of Nazianzus made him a deacon. About 385 he settled at Kellia, where he lived for fourteen years. There he wrote a system for the struggle. It sorted the tempting thoughts, the logismoi, into eight kinds. It also set out a path from practice to freedom from passion, and then to contemplation. The system belonged to him and his learned circle.

Evagrius died at Kellia in January 399. That year Theophilus, the bishop of Alexandria, sent an Easter letter saying that God has no human body. John Cassian, a monk who had lived at Scete, wrote about it decades later. He reports that almost all the monks of Egypt took the letter badly. They felt it went against Scripture, which they took to give God a human form. Theophilus then reversed course, for reasons scholars dispute. He campaigned against the followers of the teacher Origen.

In 400, a council at Alexandria condemned Origen and the monks who followed him. That year four monk leaders called the Tall Brothers, and others among them, had to leave Egypt. The circle around Evagrius was broken up.

dates.born: c. 251 (derived: Vita SS89 has him say, shortly before his death, that he is 'near a hundred and five years old'; external chronology fixes his death in 356)
dates.died: 356, at the inner mountain - narrated at Vita SS92-93, written by Athanasius shortly after
dates.floruit: withdrawal begun in his late teens or early twenties, within six months of his parents' deaths, after hearing Matthew 19:21 read aloud in church and taking it as address to himself directly (Vita SS2); the tombs, then the fort at Pispir for some twenty years (SS8-13), then the inner mountain from c. 313 until his death (SS49-50)

voices.hedge: His own biographer says he never learned to read. But a handful of letters may genuinely be his own. They suggest a more philosophically trained man than that portrait allows. The two pictures have never been reconciled.
voices.text: Antony heard one Gospel reading in church and took it as spoken to him directly. He gave away his family's land that same day. Then he withdrew in stages: first to the village's edge, then to an abandoned fort, and finally to a remote inner mountain, where he stayed for the rest of his life.

dates.died: 346 - by which point the federation he founded numbered nine houses for men and two for women, membership in the low thousands (an order-of-magnitude figure transmitted by the Lives, not a precise census)
dates.floruit: founded the first cenobitic community at Tabennesi in the Thebaid c. 318-323, most often placed c. 320 - traditionally after a vision, joined immediately by his brother John and then by further companions (the founding narrative comes down through the hagiographic Lives; its incident-level reliability has not been independently verified)

voices.hedge: Those who remembered him afterward still called him a father, not just an officeholder. They said his own example had formed the community. The population and house-count figures are a witness's rough estimate, not a precise census.
voices.text: Pachomius founded the desert's first rule-governed community at Tabennesi around 320. By his death in 346, tradition says it had grown into a federation of nine houses for men and two for women. A written rule and named offices governed it, not just one elder's own example.

voices.hedge: This world's own record accepts its era's own idea that courage is manly and weakness is womanly. It does not reject that idea outright. Sarah's own saying claims the first category for herself.
voices.text: Sarah was one of a small number of women remembered by name in this world's own teaching tradition. Six of her sayings survive. She used to say to her brothers that she was a man, and they were women.

dates.born: c. 345 (derived: Palladius ch. XXXVIII gives his age at death as fifty-four; the calendar year of his death, 399, comes from Evagrius's own Praktikos, not from the surviving chapter itself, which carries no year)
dates.died: January 399, at Kellia - communicating in church at Epiphany, per Palladius ch. XXXVIII (the year itself from desert.source.evagrius-praktikos and Doc_01 SS2.3) - shortly before the Origenist controversy that would scatter his intellectual circle broke fully open (Doc_01 SS2.3)
dates.floruit: ordained reader by Basil of Caesarea, then deacon by Gregory Nazianzen (Palladius ch. XXXVIII), at Constantinople specifically (Socrates IV.23); withdrew to Nitria, then to Kellia c. 385 for fourteen years until his death - this world's most systematic participant-author and, by education, its most atypical

voices.hedge: Within this world's own span, his standing was inheritance mixed with real unease, not condemnation. A formal, later condemnation of some of his writing came more than a century after this world's own window closes. It settles nothing about how his own circle regarded him at the time.
voices.text: Evagrius was the most formally educated man the desert produced. Basil of Caesarea ordained him a reader. Gregory of Nazianzus made him a deacon. Then he withdrew to Kellia. There, he organized this world's practical wisdom about tempting thoughts into its most complete scheme. He died in January 399, months before a controversy his own circle could not survive.

tile.text: Between about 320 and 430, Christians in Egypt left their villages for the edge of the desert. The last empire-wide persecution had ended. The tradition describes its struggle as one against demons, and the tempting thoughts they stirred in a person's mind. Monks lived in three ways. Some lived alone, as Antony did after he gave away his inheritance. Others lived in settlements such as Nitria, Kellia and Scetis. They kept small cells and gathered once a week for worship. Pachomius gathered monks into houses under a written rule. Elders guided the hermits and the settlements. A rule and appointed offices governed the Pachomian houses. These two kinds of authority stood side by side through these years. Evagrius, an educated monk at Kellia, wrote a system for sorting the thoughts a monk fights into eight kinds. He died in January 399. A controversy that began over how to picture God led to the expulsion of Origen's monk followers from Egypt in 400. It scattered Evagrius's circle.
